tasks.title: Backups that actually work
tasks.source:
Keep at least three copies of anything you cannot afford to lose: the original, a backup on a different device, and a backup in a different place.

A backup is only useful if you can restore it. Once a month, pick one file at random and restore it from each backup. If that fails, fix it today.

Do not keep your only backup connected to the computer all the time. Ransomware encrypts every drive it can reach.

tasks.title: Why use a password manager
tasks.source:
Reusing one password everywhere means one leak opens all your accounts. A password manager creates a different long password for every site and remembers it for you.

You then need to remember only one strong master password. Protect it with two-factor authentication, and write your recovery codes on paper.

Never type your master password into a page you reached from a link in an email.

tasks.title: Recognising phishing messages
tasks.source:
Phishing messages pretend to come from a bank, a delivery company or a colleague. They usually ask you to act fast: pay a fee, confirm a password or open an attachment.

Before you click a link, check where it really goes. If in doubt, open the official website or app yourself instead of using the link.

No real bank will ask for your one-time code by phone or message.

tasks.title: Storing drinking water at home
tasks.source:
Store drinking water in clean containers with tight lids, away from sunlight and chemicals.

Use containers made for food or water. Wash them with soap, rinse well, and let them dry before filling.

Replace stored water every six months, and write the filling date on each container.

tasks.title: How to report a bug in an open-source project
tasks.source:
Before you open an issue, search the existing ones: the bug may already be known.

A good bug report says what you did, what you expected, and what happened instead. Include the version you used and the smallest steps that reproduce the problem.

Be patient and polite. Most maintainers work on the project in their free time.

tasks.title: Writing clear labelling instructions
tasks.source:
Labelling instructions must be short enough that people actually read them. Give one rule per line and one example for each label.

Show the hard cases too: images where two labels both seem right, and what to choose then.

Before labelling the whole dataset, ask two people to label the same 50 samples and compare their answers.
